entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18528"/><div sID="gen39011" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18528"/><hi type="bold">3. we understand--</hi>We perceive with our spiritual intelligence the fact of the world's creation by God, though we see neither Him nor the act of creation as described in <reference osisRef="Gen.1.1-Gen.1.31">Ge 1:1-31</reference>. The natural world could not, without revelation, teach us this truth, though it confirms the truth when apprehended by faith (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.20">Ro 1:20</reference>). Adam is passed over in silence here as to his faith, perhaps as being the first who fell and brought sin on us all; though it does not follow that he did not repent and believe the promise.<div eID="gen39011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39012" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">worlds--</hi>literally, "ages"; all that exists in time and space, visible and invisible, present and eternal.<div eID="gen39012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39013" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">framed--</hi>"fitly formed and consolidated"; including the creation of the single parts and the harmonious organization of the whole, and the continual providence which maintains the whole throughout all ages. As creation is the foundation and a specimen of the whole divine economy, so faith in creation is the foundation and a specimen of all faith [Bengel].<div eID="gen39013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the word of God--</hi>not here, the personal word (Greek, "logos," <reference osisRef="John.1.1">Joh 1:1</reference>) but the spoken word (Greek, "rhema"); though by the instrumentality of the personal word (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.2">He 1:2</reference>).<div eID="gen39014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39015" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not made, &c.--</hi>Translate as Greek, "so that not out of things which appear hath that which is seen been made"; not as in the case of all things which we see reproduced from previously existing and visible materials, as, for instance, the plant from the seed, the animal from the parent, &c., has the visible world sprung into being from apparent materials. So also it is implied in the first clause of the verse that the invisible spiritual worlds were framed not from previously existing materials. Bengel explains it by distinguishing "appear," that is, begin to be seen (namely, at creation), from that which is seen as already in existence, not merely beginning to be seen; so that the things seen were not made of the things which appear," that is, which begin to be seen by us in the act of creation. We were not spectators of creation; it is by faith we perceive it. <div eID="gen39015" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18529"/><div sID="gen39016" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18529"/><hi type="bold">4. more excellent sacrifice--</hi>because offered in faith. Now faith must have some revelation of God on which it fastens. The revelation in this case was doubtless God's command to sacrifice animals ("the firstlings of the flock") in token of the forfeiture of men's life by sin, and as a type of the promised bruiser of the serpent's head (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Ge 3:15</reference>), the one coming sacrifice: this command is implied in God's having made coats of skin for Adam and Eve (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.21">Ge 3:21</reference>): for these skins must have been taken from animals slain in sacrifice: inasmuch as it was not for food they were slain, animal food not being permitted till after the flood; nor for mere clothing, as, were it so, clothes might have been made of the fleeces without the needless cruelty of killing the animal; but a coat of skin put on Adam from a sacrificed animal typified the covering or atonement (the Hebrew for atone means to cover) resulting from Christ's sacrifice. The Greek is more literally rendered [Kennicott] by Wycliffe, "a much more sacrifice"; and by Queen Elizabeth's version "a greater sacrifice." A fuller, more ample sacrifice, that which partook more largely and essentially of the true nature and virtue of sacrifice [Archbishop Magee]. It was not any intrinsic merit in "the firstling of the flock" above "the fruit of the ground." It was God's appointment that gave it all its excellency as a sacrifice; if it had not been so, it would have been a presumptuous act of will-worship (<reference osisRef="Col.2.23">Col 2:23</reference>), and taking of a life which man had no right over before the flood (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.1-Gen.9.6">Ge 9:1-6</reference>). The sacrifice seems to have been a holocaust, and the sign of the divine acceptance of it was probably the consumption of it by fire from heaven (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.17">Ge 15:17</reference>). Hence, "to accept" a burnt sacrifice is in Hebrew "to turn it to ashes" (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.3">Psa 20:3</reference>, Margin). A flame seems to have issued from the Shekinah, or flaming cherubim, east of Eden ("the presence of the Lord," <reference osisRef="Gen.4.16">Ge 4:16</reference>), where the first sacrifices were offered. Cain, in unbelieving self-righteousness, presented merely a thank offering, not like Abel feeling his need of the propitiatory sacrifice appointed on account of sin. God "had respect (first) unto Abel, and (then) to his offering" (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.4">Ge 4:4</reference>). Faith causes the believer's person to be accepted, and then his offering. Even an animal sacrifice, though of God's appointment, would not have been accepted, had it not been offered in faith.<div eID="gen39016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he obtained witness--</hi>God by fire attesting His acceptance of him as "righteous by faith."<div eID="gen39017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his gifts--</hi>the common term for sacrifices, implying that they must be freely given.<div eID="gen39018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by it--</hi>by faith exhibited in his animal sacrifice.<div eID="gen39019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dead, yet speaketh--</hi>His blood crying front the ground to God, shows how precious, because of his "faith," he was still in God's sight, even when dead. So he becomes a witness to us of the blessed effects of faith. <div eID="gen39020" type="x-p"/>

Faith answered the objections which reason brought against God's command to Abraham to offer Isaac, by suggesting that what God had promised He both could and would perform, however impossible the performance might seem (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.20">Ro 4:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.21">21</reference>).<div eID="gen39086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39087" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">able to raise him--</hi>rather, in general, "able to raise from the dead." Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.4.17">Ro 4:17</reference>, "God who quickeneth the dead." The quickening of Sarah's dead womb suggested the thought of God's power to raise even the dead, though no instance of it had as yet occurred.<div eID="gen39087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39088" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he received him--</hi>"received him back" [Alford].<div eID="gen39088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39089" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in a figure--</hi>Greek, "in a parable." Alford explains, "Received him back, risen from that death which he had undergone in, under, the figure of the ram." I prefer with Bishop Pearson, Estius, and Gregory of Nyssa, understanding the figure to be the representation which the whole scene gave to Abraham of Christ in His death (typified by Isaac's offering in intention, and the ram's actual substitution answering to Christ's vicarious death), and in His resurrection (typified by Abraham's receiving him back alive from the jaws of death, compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.9">2Co 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>); just as on the day of atonement the slain goat and the scapegoat together formed one joint rite representing Christ's death and resurrection. It was then that Abraham saw Christ's day (<reference osisRef="John.8.56">Joh 8:56</reference>): accounting God was able to raise even from the dead: from which state of the dead he received him back as a type of the resurrection in Christ. <div eID="gen39089" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18546"/><div sID="gen39092" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18546"/><hi type="bold">21. both the sons--</hi>Greek, "each of the sons" (<reference osisRef="Gen.47.29">Ge 47:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.48.8-Gen.48.20">48:8-20</reference>). He knew not Joseph's sons, and could not distinguish them by sight, yet he did distinguish them by faith, transposing his hands intentionally, so as to lay his right hand on the younger, Ephraim, whose posterity was to be greater than that of Manasseh: he also adopted these grandchildren as his own sons, after having transferred the right of primogeniture to Joseph (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.22">Ge 48:22</reference>).<div eID="gen39092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and worshipped--</hi>This did not take place in immediate connection with the foregoing, but before it, when Jacob made Joseph swear that he would bury him with his fathers in Canaan, not in Egypt. The assurance that Joseph would do so filled him with pious gratitude to God, which he expressed by raising himself on his bed to an attitude of worship. His faith, as Joseph's (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.22">He 11:22</reference>), consisted in his so confidentially anticipating the fulfilment of God's promise of Canaan to his descendants, as to desire to be buried there as his proper possession.<div eID="gen39093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">leaning upon the top of his staff--</hi><reference osisRef="Gen.47.31">Ge 47:31</reference>, Hebrew and English Version, "upon the bed's head." The Septuagint translates as Paul here. Jerome justly reprobates the notion of modern Rome, that Jacob worshipped the top of Joseph's staff, having on it an image of Joseph's power, to which Jacob bowed in recognition of the future sovereignty of his son's tribe, the father bowing to the son! The Hebrew, as translated in English Version, sets it aside: the bed is alluded to afterwards (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.2">Ge 48:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.49.33">49:33</reference>), and it is likely that Jacob turned himself in his bed so as to have his face toward the pillow, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.2">Is 38:2</reference> (there were no bedsteads in the East). Paul by adopting the Septuagint version, brings out, under the Spirit, an additional fact, namely, that the aged patriarch used his own (not Joseph's) staff to lean on in worshipping on his bed. The staff, too, was the emblem of his pilgrim state here on his way to his heavenly city (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.13">He 11:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.14">14</reference>), wherein God had so wonderfully supported him. <reference osisRef="Gen.32.10">Ge 32:10</reference>, "With my staff I passed over Jordan, and now I am become," &c. (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.12.11">Ex 12:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.6.8">Mr 6:8</reference>). In <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.47">1Ki 1:47</reference>, the same thing is said of David's "bowing on his bed," an act of adoring thanksgiving to God for God's favor to his son before death. He omits the more leading blessing of the twelve sons of Jacob; because "he plucks only the flowers which stand by his way, and leaves the whole meadow full to his readers" [Delitzsch in Alford]. <div eID="gen39094" type="x-p"/>

He was afraid, and fled from the danger where no duty called him to stay (to have stayed without call of duty would have been to tempt Providence, and to sacrifice his hope of being Israel's future deliverer according to the divine intimations; his great aim, see on <reference osisRef="Heb.11.23">He 11:23</reference>). It was in spite of the king's prohibition he left Egypt, not fearing the consequences which were likely to overtake him if he should be caught, after having, in defiance of the king, left Egypt. If he had stayed and resumed his position as adopted son of Pharaoh's daughter, his slaughter of the Egyptian would doubtless have been connived at; but his resolution to take his portion with oppressed Israel, which he could not have done had he stayed, was the motive of his flight, and constituted the "faith" of this act, according to the express statement here. Women received their dead raised--</hi>as the widow of Zarephath (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.17-1Kgs.17.24">1Ki 17:17-24</reference>). The Shunammite (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.17-2Kgs.4.35">2Ki 4:17-35</reference>). The two oldest manuscripts read. "They received women of aliens by raising their dead." <reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.24">1Ki 17:24</reference> shows that the raising of the widow's son by Elijah led her to the faith, so that he thus took her into fellowship, an alien though she was. Christ, in <reference osisRef="Luke.4.26">Lu 4:26</reference>, makes especial mention of the fact that Elijah was sent to an alien from Israel, a woman of Sarepta. Thus Paul may quote this as an instance of Elijah's faith, that at God's command he went to a Gentile city of Sidonia (contrary to Jewish prejudices), and there, as the fruit of faith, not only raised her dead son, but received her as a convert into the family of God, as Vulgate reads. Still, English Version may be the right reading.<div eID="gen39134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39135" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>Greek, "but"; in contrast to those raised again to life.<div eID="gen39135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39136" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tortured--</hi>"broken on the wheel." The fourth of the brethren (referring to <reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Da 12:2</reference>) said to King Antiochus, "To be put to death by men, is to be chosen to look onward for the hopes which are of God, to be raised up again by Him; but for thee there is no resurrection to life." Though they were so, yet "they received not the promise," that is, the final completion of "salvation" promised at Christ's coming again (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">He 9:28</reference>); "the eternal inheritance" (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.15">He 9:15</reference>). Abraham did obtain the very thing promised (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.15">He 6:15</reference>) in part, namely, blessedness in soul after death, by virtue of faith in Christ about to come. The full blessedness of body and soul shall not be till the full number of the elect shall be accomplished, and all together, no one preceding the other, shall enter on the full glory and bliss. Moreover, in another point of view, "It is probable that some accumulation of blessedness was added to holy souls, when Christ came and fulfilled all things even as at His burial many rose from the dead, who doubtless ascended to heaven with Him" [Flacius in Bengel]. The perfecting of believers in title, and in respect to conscience, took place once for all, at the death of Christ, by virtue of His being made by death perfect as Saviour. Their perfecting in soul at, and ever after Christ's death, took place, and takes place at their death. But the universal and final perfecting will not take place till Christ's coming. <div eID="gen39150" type="x-p"/>
